For forty-one years, every street in Hollins Ford was named by the same hand. Elias Marrow painted the signs in his workshop on Tanner Street, black letters on cream boards, and it was his custom to pencil his initials and the date on the back of each. This spring white reflective letters on green metal took their place.

The old boards came down because they were rotting at the edges. A county inspector found the soft wood in January, and the council had every board taken down that month, although the county's rule on reflective letters would have let them stand until they wore out. For six weeks the posts stood bare, and drivers mistook one corner for another at night, a mix-up that lasted until the new signs arrived. The boards went into storage in the depot shed, which the ambulance service takes over as its garage in November, and everything in it must be out by then.

Dora Pask, the town clerk, has asked to swap the stack into the dry corner of the shed, but the county's salt for the winter roads already fills it. The county crews struck in March over pay, so the boards were stacked in a hurry, and the two Gates, which hung nearest the river and came off softest of all, ended up at the bottom, where the roof drips. Marrow painted both of them the year he opened the workshop. Wood that soft can split under its own weight, and those two boards are carrying the whole stack.

The council will put the boards to a town meeting in October, where residents will vote on whether to hang them in the town hall or sell them for scrap. The new signs carry the county's plain letters, made larger at the post office's request.

If the vote goes against them, or simply comes too late, forty-one years of Marrow's lettering could leave the depot in a skip. Every week of rain through that roof works further into the bottom of the stack, and I doubt October will come soon enough for the two Gates.

passage:
The summer I turned twelve, Mrs. Pellow next door offered to teach me to keep bees, and that summer her bees turned up in the oddest places. Her two hives, Agatha and Bertram, stood against the fence along Tamsin Lane, in a spot she had chosen for the morning sun. She had built both of them herself long ago and meant to have two more boxes ready by August. When my mother heard, she asked her whether I would be in the way, and Mrs. Pellow put a hammer in my hand.

In July a swarm left Bertram, sailed over the lilac by the back gate, and settled on the clothesline by our back steps, right among my mother's pillowcases. I found it hanging there like a brown woollen sock, and I laughed so hard that I had to sit down on the steps. Mrs. Pellow, laughing too, fetched one of our new boxes from under the eaves of the shed, shook the pillowcase over it, and set the swarm beside the pear tree by her kitchen.

On Saturdays she sold the honey at the Brackwell market and kept the table herself. Her pitch to every customer went the same way: she held up a jar, named the hive it came from as though introducing a cousin, and winked at me over the buyer's shoulder. One morning a bee rode all the way to Brackwell in the jar crate and climbed out onto the table in time to be introduced.

In August we took away the full frames, with the sound of the hives drifting in through the screen door. When she visited her sister for a week, she left the hives in my mother's care, and every morning my mother found Agatha's bees drinking from the china duck in our birdbath. The day she came home, Mrs. Pellow climbed the ladder onto the shed roof and found two more asleep in the gutter.

She keeps them still, and they are still called Agatha and Bertram. Whenever a jar marked Bertram turns up on my mother's table, I grin all over again at that swarm hanging among the pillowcases.

passage:
Mara Quill had owned Rook since April, when a gray shepherd mix at the Halvering County shelter sat down on her sneaker as if he had been expecting her. He kept that habit, sitting on people's feet whenever he could. In August she entered him in the Novice class of the county obedience trial, held on the fair's last morning, hours before the closing fireworks. The hard part was the recall. Rook had to stay where she left him across the ring until she called, and in practice he kept getting up early and trotting over before she said a word.

Mara practised at Linden Park, beside the field where her brother Theo's soccer team met and across the road from the fairgrounds, where workers tested the loudspeaker every afternoon. When Rook kept breaking, she emptied the liver treats out of her jacket and left them in the car. Rook broke just as often. At the shelter's Tuesday class, Mrs. Ostrander, the trainer, watched one recall and told Mara to give the command more softly. Mara had been barking "Stay!" so hard that Rook seemed to take it as the start of a game. Within days of the change he was holding every stay.

On the last practice evening, Theo was bouncing a tennis ball off the fence, and between one lazy pitch and the next, Mara asked him for a favor at the fair. He was to carry the old gray blanket and keep it by the car, ready to drape over Rook's crate the minute the fireworks began. Rook had never heard fireworks, and the fair always closed with an hour of them.

At the trial, the loudspeaker boomed out class numbers while Mara gave the stay command in a near whisper, kept one hand low against her leg, and walked away. Rook held until she called, and the judge awarded him a green ribbon. As they packed up, Theo asked whether they could watch the fireworks from the grandstand. "Let's get Rook into his covered crate in the car before the first one goes off, because one loud bang tonight could undo his whole summer."

passage:
Every September, a little before dark, the chimney swifts of Wenbury gather over the old Linden Row School, after a day of feeding along the far bank of the River Wenn. The first evening I watched them, I took the circling flock for smoke from the school's furnace, which has been cold for eleven years. The sun drops behind Calder Ridge and the church clock strikes seven while the birds wheel overhead. As the last children leave the schoolyard, the first swifts drop into the chimney, and by the time the streetlights on the hill come on and the last bus passes the school gates, most of them are inside.

Tomas Reyburn was caretaker at Linden Row for thirty years, and he lit that furnace every winter morning until the day the school closed. Since 1996 he has stood in the schoolyard each September evening with a hand counter, and his totals fill four notebooks. This year's best, 6,140, is the largest roost he has ever recorded. The council has asked to see every page of the notebooks before it meets in January.

The storm two winters ago opened a crack from the chimney's top toward the roofline, and every month since, Reyburn has gone up the roof ladder to pencil a mark at its lower end. Each new mark sits a little below the last. In January the council will vote on whether to pay for a repair in lime mortar, which the masons say the old brick needs in place of cheap cement, or to have the chimney pulled down. Reyburn expects the vote to go the swifts' way.

I am less sure. If the vote goes the other way, or a winter gale finds the crack first, the swifts will come back in May to an empty patch of sky above a heap of brick.

In early October the birds will leave for the south. On every windy night since the storm I have lain awake listening for the sound of falling brick from the hill, and each morning I look out to see whether the chimney is still standing.
